doc.title: Ben Sidran interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, November 15, 2023

title: Telling musicians what to do; rock versus jazz; quitting a band
summary: Playing with Tony Williams and Richard Davis, rock as theater versus jazz as truth, and quitting a CBS England production after four weeks.

story.theme_name: Radio and television work: staff jobs, shows and broadcasts
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Yeah, speaking of critical, have you been in a situation where you really felt you had to tell the supporting musicians that for instance they’re overplaying, let’s keep it basic? I guess I’m thinking of bass players and drummers especially.

Well yes and no. I mean I was very lucky, I got to play with Blue Mitchell. I got to play with great musicians. And even, I mean I cut some tracks at one point with Richard Davis and Tony Williams. We did it as a trio. And I was at one point talking to Tony about what I was hearing. And in the back of my head it’s you can’t tell Tony Williams, who do you think you are? But it’s defused when you’re talking about the music. So it’s not a problem. But I have had the experience for example of working with, see as you can tell I have a real distinction between rock & roll, commercial music, and jazz. I think they shouldn’t even be in the same sentence. Because most rock & roll music is theater. It’s a lie. Quite frankly it’s a lie. The Rolling Stones for example are not “street fighting men,” but that was the presentation, right? Rock & roll is a lie. It’s theater, but anyway, jazz is a truth. It’s the deepest truth I think. And I came along at a time when you had to participate in the world of pop music. It’s the only world that was. If you look back at the

late ‘60s, early ‘70s, jazz was dead in the water. There were no gigs, there was nothing going on. So you either got involved in pop music or you didn’t, you didn’t work a lot. And I was working as a producer at one point for the CBS Columbia Records arm in England. And they assigned this band to me as a producer, and go produce this band. And after four weeks I went back to the company and say I quit. I said I quit. There’s not a record in these people. You know we’re sitting here in this room and they want me to write their song for them. Well some producers are happy to do that. That’s not who I am, I’m not going to write your song. I’m going to try my best to capture your song but I’m not going to manufacture your song. And the person I said it to said to me, “Ben, don’t do that. Don’t. Finish. Get a record out of here one way or the other, that’s what a producer does.” And so the road forked for me there. I realized well I’m not that, whatever that is, I can’t do that. I don’t know how to live with myself and do that. It’s like I’m making sausage at that point and I don’t know how to make sausage in a recording studio.
